newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Coffee up, cocoa down in active commodities.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Coffee up, cocoa down in active commodities.

text.p: World coffee prices jumped on Tuesday with London futures up almost eight percent on the day in a sudden return to the market by speculative buyers.

Coffee had retreated after its dramatic rally recently - it hit a 20-year high in New York last month - but Tuesday's abrupt jump suggested that concerns about tight Latin American supply still lingered.
London robusta coffee futures ended the day up $132 on the September contract at $1,910 per tonne.
Coffee's recent rally was largely driven by concerns about tight Latin American supply, particularly in Brazil, the biggest seller.
Although no damaging cold is expected this week in the Brazil coffee belt, recent wet weather could become a concern because of the impact on harvesting.
New York's most active September arabica coffee futures contract rose at one point by more than seven cents to $1.89 per pound on Tuesday.
Traders there cited speculative buying against a backdrop of lower-than-expected stock data.

The Green Coffee Association of New York reported that U.S. coffee warehouse stocks rose in May by 122,000 60-kg bags, to 1,977,000 bags. Most industry participants expected a build of 150,000-250,000 bags.
The cocoa market turned in an early speculative rally to
hit new eight-year highs in New York, only to finish the session lower on a wave of U.S. profit-taking that spilled over into London.

Concerns about next season's crop in top producer Ivory Coast and worries about a developing El Nino weather pattern had driven hefty gains in cocoa prices last week and continue to overhang the market.
In the past, dryness in the southern hemisphere has been one result of El Nino. The 1983 El Nino caused severe drought in Indonesia, the world's third-largest cocoa producer.
But benchmark London cocoa futures eased by 11 pounds sterling to a close at 1,112 pounds for September as the selloff spurred heavy speculative liquidation in long positions.
Crude oil was boosted on worries about supply and Middle East tension, pushing shorts to cover their positions.

News that Iran had successfully tested an air-launched anti-ship missile last month and that Washington had warned the Islamic republic against any attempt to halt shipping in the Gulf unsettled the market.
Continued uncertainty about when Iraq would begin crude exports under the second term of its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations also supported the market.
In other world commodity markets, industrial metals put in a weak performance on the London Metal Exchange, but managed to scrape themselves off their session lows.
Gold and silver markets edged higher, with silver testing the upside, while platinum and palladium both ticked lower.
Bullion was fixed in London at $342.30 an ounce compared $341.50 on Monday afternoon.
Experts at a Financial Times Gold Conference in Prague painted an ominous picture for gold's long term prospects marked by lower prices and a lack of investment interest.
"This is the most negative sentiment I have ever seen at these events," said Stewart Murray, chief executive to the gold indutry's leading market research group, Gold Fields Minerals Services.

In other precious metals news the Russian finance ministry said the country would not fully liberalise its gold market before mid-1998 and had no plans to open up its platinum group metals market. Russia recently announced plans to allow domestic commercial banks to export gold freely, which would require legislative changes.
Platinum and palladium softened early in the day on a fresh Russian statement on long delayed exports.

Yuri Kotlyar, the first deputy chief executive of Norilsk Nickel -- Russia's largest producer of platinum and palladium -- was quoted by Itar-Tass news agency saying exports would resume later this month.
A Norilsk spokesman later said the company was producing about 70 percent of the amount of platinum and palladium concentrates it did during its peak 1989-1990, but did not give production volumes.
